clinicalPearls: A distally obstructed fallopian tube that becomes distended with serous fluid, most often as a late sequela of previous tubal inflammation
Frequently follows pelvic inflammatory disease, endometriosis, or prior pelvic or tubal surgery, and may be asymptomatic
When symptomatic it can cause chronic pelvic pain, an intermittent watery vaginal discharge, or subfertility
Ultrasound typically shows a tubular fluid-filled structure with incomplete septa, and cross-sectional beak or cogwheel appearances
The fluid within a hydrosalpinx is thought to be embryotoxic and can reflux into the uterine cavity, impairing implantation
Its presence markedly reduces the success of in vitro fertilisation, and treating it beforehand improves pregnancy rates
Salpingectomy or proximal tubal occlusion of the affected tube is recommended prior to assisted conception to remove the detrimental effect
reference.pathophysiology: Inflammatory damage to the fimbrial end of the fallopian tube leads to distal occlusion. The tubal epithelium continues to secrete fluid, which, unable to escape, accumulates and progressively dilates the tube. The retained fluid is believed to be embryotoxic and can flow retrogradely into the endometrial cavity, both mechanically disturbing and biochemically impairing embryo implantation, which explains the adverse effect of hydrosalpinx on natural and assisted conception.
additionalInvestigations: Transvaginal ultrasound showing a tubular fluid collection with incomplete septa
Hysterosalpingography to assess tubal patency and demonstrate distal blockage
Magnetic resonance imaging to characterise a complex or large adnexal fluid collection
Laparoscopy with chromopertubation, which allows both diagnosis and treatment
Assessment for coexisting tubal or pelvic disease before planning fertility treatment
redFlags: Features of superimposed infection, such as a pyosalpinx or tubo-ovarian abscess with pain and fever
Acute severe pain suggesting torsion of the distended tube
Rapidly enlarging or complex adnexal mass raising other concerns
Systemic upset indicating active pelvic infection
reference.prognosis: Hydrosalpinx itself is benign but is an important cause of subfertility; addressing the affected tube before in vitro fertilisation restores implantation and pregnancy rates towards those of women without tubal disease.
pitfalls: Proceeding to in vitro fertilisation without treating a hydrosalpinx and thereby reducing success
Mistaking a hydrosalpinx for an ovarian cyst on imaging
Overlooking the possibility of superimposed infection
Failing to counsel on the fertility implications and treatment options
management: Laparoscopic salpingectomy or proximal tubal occlusion of the affected tube before in vitro fertilisation to remove embryotoxic fluid and restore implantation rates
Tubal reconstructive surgery such as neosalpingostomy in selected women wishing to attempt natural conception
Ultrasound-guided aspiration of hydrosalpinx fluid at oocyte retrieval when surgery is declined or not feasible
Identification and treatment of coexisting pelvic pathology such as endometriosis or adhesions
Symptomatic management of chronic pelvic pain or watery vaginal discharge
Referral to fertility services for assisted conception after definitive tubal treatment
